extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate students in mathematics studying maxima/minima and the calculus of variations
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of existence, characterization, and methods for maxima/minima problems in finite and infinite dimensional settings (Steiner/isoperimetric problems, calculus of variations, minimal surfaces), including illustrative examples and physical experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weierstrass extreme value principle / compactness criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: In a compact domain a continuous function attains a largest and smallest value (Weierstrass’ theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To guarantee existence of a maximum and a minimum for a quantity depending continuously on the position in a domain, restrict the domain to be compact (e.g. enclose an unbounded plane by a large circle and consider its interior plus boundary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonexistence on noncompact domains
rubrics_metrics.description: If the domain of the independent variable is not bounded (not compact), the extremum problem may have no solution (neither minimum nor maximum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: two unbounded curves may have lower bound 0 and upper bound infinity with neither attained; for problems on infinite domains artificially restricting the domain (|x| < R) can produce extrema that move to infinity as R increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundary versus interior extrema distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Extreme values attained at the boundary of the domain are not genuine 'free' extrema: they are not extrema relative to a full two-sided neighborhood and change when the domain is extended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Free extrema persist under small variations of the independent variable in the domain; boundary extrema typically depend on the imposed boundary conditions and may yield qualitatively different solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence difficulties in infinite-dimensional variational problems
rubrics_metrics.description: In variational problems where the independent element is a whole curve or surface, existence may fail because the admissible set is not compact or the functional is not continuous on the admissible set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious: admissible sequences can converge to limits not in the admissible set (e.g. paths tending to a straight segment that is not admissible), so elementary finite-dimensional existence arguments may not apply; additional existence proofs are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discontinuous dependence example: curve length functional
rubrics_metrics.description: The length of a curve is not a continuous function of the curve (counterexample: zigzag polygons P_n of length 2d converge to segment AB of length d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume continuous dependence of geometric functionals on shapes; this affects existence and limiting arguments in variational problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convexity of optimal isoperimetric curves
rubrics_metrics.description: A closed curve of prescribed length that encloses the maximum possible area must be convex: the straight segment joining any two points of the curve lies inside or on the curve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the curve were nonconvex one can reflect an exterior arc across a chord to obtain a curve of the same length but larger area, contradicting maximality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetry / equal-arc division consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: If C is a maximizing curve of length L, choosing two points A, B that divide C into arcs of equal length yields that the line AB must divide the area into equal parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Otherwise reflecting the larger part across AB increases area; this symmetry reduction leads to a subproblem whose solution is a semicircle, implying the whole maximizing curve is a circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular polygon maximizes area among 2n-gons of fixed perimeter
rubrics_metrics.description: Among all 2n-gons with the same perimeter, the regular 2n-gon has the largest area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof pattern: existence follows from continuity on a compact set, P must be convex; adjacent unequal edges can be replaced by an isosceles triangle with larger area, forcing all edges equal; show vertices lie on a circle to conclude regularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isoperimetric inequality (plane)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any closed plane curve of length L and enclosed area A, the inequality A ≤ L^2/(4π) holds, with equality only for the circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expresses the isoperimetric property of the circle and quantifies the maximum-area criterion for fixed perimeter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isoperimetric property in three dimensions / sphere criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Among closed three-dimensional bodies with given surface area A, the sphere maximizes enclosed volume V; equality in the corresponding inequality holds only for the sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete, rigorous proof is harder (first given by H. A. Schwarz); the 3D isoperimetric relation expresses the sphere’s extremal property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative types of solutions under boundary constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: When domain variability is restricted by boundary conditions, extremum problems often have two alternative types of solutions: interior (free) extrema or extrema attained on the boundary, yielding qualitatively different minimizers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Schwarz’s triangle problem (interior altitude triangle vs boundary altitude counted twice) and Steiner’s three-village problem (interior Fermat point with three 120° angles vs boundary vertex solution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modified isoperimetric with prescribed interior points — topology and limiting behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: If closed curves of prescribed area A must include/passthrough fixed points P,Q,R and L is minimized, solutions vary with A: for large A a circle; as A decreases solutions become convex circular triangles of equal-radius arcs, then concave circular triangles, then configurations with doubly counted straight segments, and as A→0 the Steiner problem is recovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topology and geometry of minimizers can change as constraint parameters vary; analyze limiting processes to relate constrained isoperimetric and Steiner problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fermat principle in optics (variational formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: In an inhomogeneous medium, a light ray traveling between two points follows a path along which the time taken is a minimum among all paths joining the two points (Fermat principle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This minimum-time principle can be used to derive Snell’s law and is the physical basis for variational approaches in optics and for using slab discretization arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bernoulli slab discretization method (heuristic for brachistochrone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dissect the medium/vertical distance into thin horizontal slabs and approximate the variational problem by a finite problem where in each slab the path is straight; apply the local minimum (refraction) principle across slabs and pass to the limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads to the refraction-type equalities sin α_n / √n d = constant and characterizes the cycloid; useful heuristic but requires justification for existence and limiting passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization condition for the brachistochrone / cycloid
rubrics_metrics.description: For the brachistochrone curve C, if α is the angle of the tangent with the vertical at point P and h is the vertical distance from the start, then sin α / √h is constant along C; this property characterizes the cycloid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from the slab/refraction heuristic; rigorous justification needs care about existence and convergence of approximate solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geodesics on the sphere and maxi-min problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Shortest arcs between two non-antipodal points on a sphere are shorter great-circle arcs; longer great-circle arcs provide solutions to certain maxi-min problems when a path is constrained to pass through an intermediate point S and one seeks to maximize the minimal length PSQ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalize to paths constrained to pass through prescribed points; the maximizing choice of intermediate points yields great-circle paths that may wind around the sphere multiple times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plateau’s minimal surface (mean curvature zero) criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A surface of least area bounded by a given closed contour (Plateau’s problem) is a minimal surface whose mean curvature at every point is zero; minimal surfaces are saddle-shaped and satisfy associated partial differential equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existence proofs for general contours are nontrivial (Douglas and Rado provided general existence results); soap-film experiments provide physical realizations but are not rigorous proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soap-film empirical criteria: meeting angles and stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Soap films spanning wire frames form minimal surfaces that meet along intersection lines at 120° and can realize a variety of topologies (e.g., several nearly plane surfaces in a cube frame).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Soap-film experiments are useful to visualize and 'solve' Plateau-type problems experimentally; they reveal phenomena like multiple stable relative minima, topology changes, and configurations with doubly counted segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topological multiplicity and stability in minimal-surface problems
rubrics_metrics.description: For some boundary contours there can be multiple stable minimal surfaces of different topological type (e.g., a disk and a one-sided Möbius strip) serving as relative minima; which forms are realized depends on area/energy comparisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deforming the boundary can produce sudden topological transitions; ranges of boundary shapes may admit coexistence of distinct stable solutions.
